# Design decisions and the principle behind them {#sec-principled-decisions}

**Every architectural decision in ISLA was made by one rule: an accuracy
gain is not accepted when it is known to come from a violation of a
physical principle.** A surrogate for a boundary-value problem should
depend on the geometry, the boundary conditions and the physics, and on
nothing else; when a change improves the score by reading the mesher's cell
pattern, the sampling density, or a statistic of the drawn sample, the
improvement is a fit to the discretization, and it will not survive a
different mesher, a different sampling law, or a geometry the training set
did not contain. This appendix records each decision of that kind, the
alternative it rejected, what the alternative would have bought on the
in-distribution metric, and the evidence that located the gain in the
discretization rather than in the physics. It exists so that the paper on
ISLA can say *why* the architecture is what it is, and so that the position
is stated plainly for others: if the community wants highly generalizable
physics surrogates, it has to be willing to leave measured accuracy on the
table when that accuracy is known to be non-physical. Not everything that
is measured counts, and not everything that counts can be measured.^[The
aphorism is William Bruce Cameron's (*Informal Sociology*, 1963); it is
often misattributed to Einstein.]

## The criterion, and how it was audited {#sec-principled-criterion}

The operational form of the principle is consistency in the fine-mesh limit
(@sec-principle): under uniform refinement of the sampled boundary the
prediction converges to one field, and a dependence on the sampling
distribution that does not vanish with refinement is a defect, however much
it improves a score at a fixed cell count. A falling error with more cells
is not a defect; a different answer under a different sampler at every
count is. Two questions were asked of every proposed change, before and
after it was measured: *why should this work*, in mechanistic terms, and
would a practitioner of classical CFD look at the construction without
objecting to what it consumes. Changes that could not answer both were
run, when they were run at all, as ablations and are labelled so wherever
they appear. Past changes were audited by the same questions after the rule
was written (@sec-nb-principle-redirect), and two were reversed as a result.

## The ledger {#sec-principled-ledger}

Each row names the decision as it stands in the reference configuration,
the rejected alternative, what the alternative measured on the
in-distribution surface-pressure metric (float32, seed means; a ratio
below one means the alternative scored better), what the alternative
consumed that the physics does not provide, and the evidence. Every number
is stated in the chapters it points to and carries its artifact there.

| Decision (reference) | Rejected alternative | What the alternative would have bought | What it reads that the physics does not provide | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Quadrature (measure) weights in the routing softmax | Unweighted routing, the "weights-off" configuration | 8–17% on the HiLift wing rungs, 3% on DrivAerML at 10,000 cells | The number of cells the mesher placed in a region. Under area-proportional sampling the unweighted model's error rises to 0.66–1.29, worse than predicting zero; on the wings its advantage is flat in cell count, the signature of mesh-pattern content | @sec-limits-mechanism, @sec-consistency-bench, @sec-nb-bench-verdict, @sec-nb-overfit-routing-probe |
| Frame-free relative frame: positions enter only as differences against slice anchors | Constant gauge: centre on the plain mean of the sampled points | Nothing on DrivAerML; 1–5% on never-seen-geometry wing rungs; 11% where validation geometries recur in training; 14.5% at the fixed angle | The mesher's refinement pattern, through the plain mean's offset from the geometric centroid (0.13 body lengths on the wings). Under a 10:1 sampling bias the constant gauge degrades 12–16x; an exact full-geometry frame with every positional seed pays *more* than the frame-free construction (14–16% at 35 cases, 21% at the fixed angle), so the price is the pattern, not positional information | @sec-nb-frame-full-verdict, @sec-nb-frame-full-fixed-angle-verdict, @sec-nb-relframe-ladder-verdict |
| Frame-free relative frame | Similarity gauge: Horvitz–Thompson centroid and RMS radius estimated from the sample | 3–9% where validation geometries recur (35 and 210 cases); nothing on DrivAerML or at 4 geometries and the fixed angle, where the reference is at parity or better | An absolute position on a wing that recurs between training and deployment; an estimated frame is a sample statistic even when consistent under refinement, and the gain is a fit to a fixed fleet of shapes | @sec-nb-relframe-ladder-verdict, @sec-nb-relframe-verdict |
| Length unit from the total surface measure, $L=(\sum_i w_i)^{1/2}$ | A constant `reference_length` per dataset | Nothing: the constant-length relative frame pays 22–26% at the fixed angle against the total-measure arm's 10–14.5% | A per-dataset constant that has to be chosen by hand and encodes the fleet's size; the integral of the geometry is consistent under Horvitz–Thompson weights and needs no choice | @sec-nb-relframe-ladder-fixed-angle, @sec-nb-frame-full-fixed-angle-verdict |
| Uniform interior query law in training | Far-wake oversampling of the training queries with exact inclusion weights | Nothing: every band of every field worse; far-shell eddy viscosity 0.193 against 0.118 | A training query distribution that differs from the deployment one; the interacting decode's prediction depends on the joint query set, so a training-time sampling law is not a deployable remedy | @sec-nb-farwake-verdict, @sec-interior-task |
| Deploy the interacting decode at the training query count | Query-count augmentation as the flagship | A 40% reduction of the query-count dependence at a 3.7% cost | Nothing non-physical, but the dependence is intrinsic to an interacting decode and is stated rather than papered over; augmentation stays a documented mitigation | @sec-nb-qcount-verdict, @sec-interior-companion |
| One configuration for every dataset and task | Per-dataset reference configurations chosen by a rung-count rule | Up to 17% on individual wing rungs by picking the discretization-reading configuration where it wins | Knowledge of which dataset a case comes from; a surrogate that changes its construction per dataset has no claim to generalize across them | @sec-principle, @sec-nb-principle-redirect |
| Report every comparison with matched inputs in float32 | The original protocol: physical freestream velocity for the baselines, bfloat16 scoring | A 2.8x headline advantage at 35 cases and a 3–10% flattering offset everywhere | An input-scale artifact in the baselines' global projector and a precision artifact that fell unevenly across architectures | @sec-part-baseline, @sec-nb-fp32-drivaer-regrade |
| Present ISLA as a new architecture; leave GeoTransolver and Transolver as released | Back-port measure weighting and the geometric frame into the released baselines | Sampler-consistent baselines at unchanged accuracy (1.03–1.04x under the density bias) | Nothing non-physical; the released architectures are stable and in use, so their measure-consistent variants stay research diagnostics that locate a property, never shipped modifications | @sec-nb-mwaw-verdict, @sec-nb-ruling-released-baselines |

Two rows deserve a sentence each, because they are the ones where the
principle cost the most.

The **measure weights** are the clearest case. With them, a slice state is
a quadrature estimate of a surface integral; without them it is a mean over
whichever points the mesher happened to place, and the network learns the
mesher. The price on the wings is real and understood: part of it is the
estimator variance of a quadrature-weighted mean over a heavy-tailed draw
of cell areas, which shrinks with cell count and is nearly gone at 40,000
cells on the cars; the rest is mesh-pattern content in the ablation, which
does not shrink and which collapses the moment the sampling law changes.
An accuracy table at one cell count cannot tell these apart. The
consistency benchmark can, and it decided.

The **frame** is the case where the trade was closest, and it is stated
without softening. Where the same wings recur between training and
validation, an estimated centre and scale are worth 3–9% against the
frame-free construction, and at 210 recurring cases the Horvitz–Thompson
frame meets the accuracy condition this program had set for accepting it.
It was still declined, because the rungs that test geometries the model has
never seen favour the frame-free construction, and because an estimated
frame is a statistic of the sample even when it is a consistent one. For a
fixed fleet of shapes the gauge is the better instrument; the reference
configuration is built for the shapes that have not been seen yet.

## What we would ask of the field {#sec-principled-ask}

Three practices follow from the ledger, and none of them is expensive.

- **Measure consistency, not only accuracy.** Score every model under at
  least two sampling laws and at more than one cell count, and report
  whether the answers converge to each other. A model that is 10% better at
  10,000 cells and 10x worse under a different sampler has learned the
  mesher (@sec-consistency-bench).
- **Locate every gain before adopting it.** When a change improves the
  score, run the test that would reveal a discretization dependence, and
  ask what the change consumes that the physics does not supply. A
  mechanism that cannot be stated is a hypothesis; a gain whose mechanism
  is the mesh is not a gain.
- **Pre-register the bar and keep the refuted configurations runnable.**
  Every decision above was made against a bar written before the run, and
  every rejected alternative remains in the code as a labelled ablation so
  that the price can be re-measured when the data or the metric change.

The accuracy metric is one number about one discretization of one dataset.
It is necessary and it is not sufficient, and a research programme that
optimizes it alone will converge on surrogates that know their mesher
better than their physics.
